pathway.title: Software Development
pathway.description: Develop maintainable systems by connecting domain models, architecture, persistence, quality automation, threat modelling, observability, release, and evolution.

course.title: Software Development — Intermediate
course.short_description: An intermediate software-development course focused on domain modelling, architecture, APIs, persistence, asynchronous workflows, configuration, testing strategy, CI, threat modelling, operations, releases, and refactoring.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Software Development — Beginner or equivalent experience with requirements, modular Python, version control, tests, debugging, and basic release documentation.
learning_outcomes: Refine requirements into domain models, invariants, architecture boundaries, and API contracts.
Design persistence and asynchronous workflows with explicit compatibility and failure policies.
Build risk-based testing strategies and repeatable CI evidence.
Threat-model systems and design secure, observable, operable services.
Plan progressive releases, recovery, architecture decisions, and evidence-based refactoring.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

topics.title: Refine requirements into domain models and invariants
topics.description: Domain modelling identifies concepts, relationships, rules, and invariants before implementation.

lesson.title: Refine requirements into domain models and invariants
objectives: Keep domain rules separate from infrastructure.
Turn examples and counterexamples into testable behavior.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Domain modelling identifies concepts, relationships, rules, and invariants before implementation. An invariant is a condition that should remain true, such as a task title being non-blank or an order total never being negative. Separate domain rules from presentation and persistence so the core can be tested without infrastructure. Models should express meaningful behavior, not become bags of unrelated fields. Record examples and counterexamples in the language of the domain, then turn them into acceptance tests. A model is useful when it reduces ambiguity and gives developers a shared vocabulary for discussing changes. Intermediate software development connects individual coding skills to systems that other people must understand, change, test, and operate. Begin with a visible contract: state the input, output, invariants, failure behavior, and quality constraints. Choose boundaries that localize change and make dependencies replaceable. A design is a hypothesis, so use examples, tests, review, and measurements to learn whether it works. Avoid adopting a framework or pattern merely because it is fashionable; explain the trade-off and the simpler alternative. When a system handles persistence, concurrency, configuration, or external input, make ownership and failure recovery explicit. Keep sensitive data out of examples and logs, and document what has not been verified. Intermediate practice is successful when a developer can trace a requirement through design, implementation, verification, release evidence, and a maintenance plan.

topics.title: Choose architectures and boundaries deliberately
topics.description: Architecture describes important boundaries, dependencies, and runtime responsibilities.

lesson.title: Choose architectures and boundaries deliberately
objectives: Describe a boundary and dependency direction.
Explain dependency inversion in practical terms.
Evaluate the cost of adding a boundary.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Architecture describes important boundaries, dependencies, and runtime responsibilities. Layered, hexagonal, and modular-monolith approaches are useful vocabulary, not templates to apply blindly. Keep domain logic independent from adapters when the business rules deserve isolated tests. Dependency inversion means high-level policy does not depend directly on a replaceable detail; both depend on a stable abstraction. Draw a dependency direction diagram and identify where data is translated. A good architecture makes likely changes local, but every boundary has cost in code, coordination, and cognitive load. topics.title: Design APIs, compatibility, and error contracts
topics.description: An API is a promise to callers, whether it is a function, module, command, or HTTP endpoint.

lesson.title: Design APIs, compatibility, and error contracts
objectives: Define input, output, and failure contracts.
Avoid leaking implementation details through APIs.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: An API is a promise to callers, whether it is a function, module, command, or HTTP endpoint. Define valid inputs, outputs, errors, idempotency, ordering, and compatibility expectations. Stable APIs avoid leaking internal representations that callers will accidentally depend on. Choose error types and messages that help a caller respond without exposing secrets. Version or deprecate deliberately when a breaking change is necessary. Contract tests can verify that an implementation satisfies the interface while allowing different adapters behind it. topics.title: Persist data with transactions and migration thinking
topics.description: Persistence is a boundary where domain state becomes durable representation.

lesson.title: Persist data with transactions and migration thinking
objectives: Separate repository translation from domain logic.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Persistence is a boundary where domain state becomes durable representation. A repository should translate rather than spread SQL or file formats through the domain. Transactions define which changes become visible together; constraints protect invariants when multiple callers or processes exist. Schema changes need a migration plan, compatibility window, rollback or recovery approach, and data validation. Treat serialization formats as APIs: version them when necessary and decide how unknown or missing fields behave. A local database example is useful, but operational claims must match the environment actually tested. topics.title: Coordinate asynchronous workflows and reliable messaging
topics.description: Asynchronous workflows separate requesting work from completing it, but they introduce ordering, duplication, retries, visibility, and cancellation concerns.

lesson.title: Coordinate asynchronous workflows and reliable messaging
objectives: Design for duplicate delivery and retries.
Make failure and observability paths explicit.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Asynchronous workflows separate requesting work from completing it, but they introduce ordering, duplication, retries, visibility, and cancellation concerns. A message should carry enough identity for tracing and deduplication. Consumers should be idempotent when delivery may repeat. Timeouts and dead-letter or failure paths must be observable. In-process asyncio can demonstrate coordination, while a real broker adds operational concerns that must not be claimed without deployment evidence. Choose synchronous behavior when it is simpler and latency or reliability requirements do not justify asynchronous complexity. topics.title: Manage configuration, environments, and secrets
topics.description: Configuration changes between development, test, and production, but source code should not contain secrets.

lesson.title: Manage configuration, environments, and secrets
objectives: Document defaults, rotation, and operational ownership.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Configuration changes between development, test, and production, but source code should not contain secrets. Define required settings, safe defaults, validation, and ownership. Environment variables are one delivery mechanism, not a complete secret-management strategy. Fail fast for missing required configuration while giving operators an actionable, non-sensitive error. Keep environment-specific behavior visible and testable. Configuration compatibility is part of release work: document names, types, defaults, rotation expectations, and whether a change requires restart or migration. blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A testing strategy balances fast unit tests, focused integration tests, and a small number of end-to-end checks. Test doubles such as fakes and mocks can isolate a boundary, but over-mocking can make tests pass while integration is broken. Keep tests deterministic, independent, and readable. topics.title: Threat-model systems and manage operational risk
topics.description: Threat modelling asks what assets matter, who can affect them, which boundaries are exposed, and what controls reduce risk.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Threat modelling asks what assets matter, who can affect them, which boundaries are exposed, and what controls reduce risk. Use a lightweight method such as assets, actors, entry points, threats, mitigations, and residual risk. Apply secure defaults, input validation, least privilege, safe logging, dependency updates, and recovery planning. Reliability risks also matter: overload, data loss, dependency failure, and operator mistakes. Record assumptions and revisit the model when architecture or data changes. topics.description: Intermediate teams need a sustainable way to change systems.

lesson.title: Evolve systems through refactoring and architecture decisions

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Intermediate teams need a sustainable way to change systems. Refactoring should be incremental, protected by behavior tests, and connected to a reason such as reducing coupling or improving operability. An architecture decision record captures context, options, decision, consequences, and revisit triggers. Technical debt is not automatically bad; it becomes risky when hidden, unbounded, or inconsistent with current requirements. Review the system after delivery using defect data, operational evidence, and developer feedback, then choose the next improvement deliberately. Intermediate software development connects individual coding skills to systems that other people must understand, change, test, and operate. Begin with a visible contract: state the input, output, invariants, failure behavior, and quality constraints. Choose boundaries that localize change and make dependencies replaceable. A design is a hypothesis, so use examples, tests, review, and measurements to learn whether it works. Avoid adopting a framework or pattern merely because it is fashionable; explain the trade-off and the simpler alternative. When a system handles persistence, concurrency, configuration, or external input, make ownership and failure recovery explicit. Keep sensitive data out of examples and logs, and document what has not been verified. Intermediate practice is successful when a developer can trace a requirement through design, implementation, verification, release evidence, and a maintenance plan.

blocks.title: Maintainable Task Service: Design to Operations
blocks.purpose: Develop an intermediate offline task service that demonstrates domain modelling, architecture boundaries, persistence, testing strategy, automation, threat modelling, observability, release planning, and sustainable maintenance.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional task data only; do not collect names, contact details, credentials, or learner identifiers.
Keep the project offline and use in-memory or SQLite demonstrations. Do not claim multi-user deployment, backups, or production monitoring were verified.
Use Python 3.10+ standard library only and document all unverified operational assumptions.
requirements: Define a domain model with at least two invariants and a documented error contract.
Separate domain, application service, repository, and entry-point responsibilities behind small interfaces.
Implement add, search, complete, and repeat-safe operations with persistence or a clearly justified in-memory adapter.
Create unit, integration, and contract-test evidence matched to identified risks.
Provide configuration validation, safe logging, a lightweight threat model, and no embedded secrets.
Write a CI checklist and release plan with measurable gates, staged exposure, and rollback or recovery reasoning.
Include a runbook, architecture decision record, README, and prioritized technical-debt note.
suggested_steps: Model concepts, invariants, API contracts, and risks.
Draw the architecture and implement a thin vertical slice with a fake repository.
Add persistence, transaction tests, and contract/integration evidence.
Add configuration, threat model, CI evidence, observability, and runbook.
Prepare staged release and refactoring plans, then review limitations.
success_checks: Domain invariants and error behavior are explicit and tested.
Replaceable boundaries allow focused tests without infrastructure.
Persistence or adapter behavior is verified with integration evidence.
CI, threat, observability, release, rollback, and runbook artifacts are actionable.
The project is reproducible, privacy-aware, and honest about unverified production assumptions.

rubric.look_for: Clear invariants, contracts, responsibility boundaries, dependency direction, and decision record.

Risk-based unit, integration, contract evidence and repeatable CI checks.
Threat model, safe logs, runbook, observability, release gates, and recovery reasoning.
README, compatibility assumptions, staged delivery, refactoring plan, and technical-debt priorities.
